### Question 1

Two different questions get asked about any treatment. The first is 'did it work?' - that is effectiveness. The second is 'did the process of delivering it injure the patient?' - that is safety. A treatment can succeed clinically and still injure someone along the way, which is why safety gets measured on its own terms. The WHO wording adds a second layer: besides erasing preventable injuries, keep driving down the leftover risk that remains even when everything is done right.

### Question 2

Think of a bike shop. You bring the bike in because the chain slips; if the chain still slips when you leave, that is the problem you arrived with. But if you leave with a scratch the mechanic's tool put on the frame, that is new damage the shop caused. An adverse event is that second thing: an injury traceable to the help itself. Both pieces have to be there - real harm, and a line you can draw from the care to the harm - which is why a rule broken with no injury is classified differently.

### Question 3

Different bodies hold different kinds of power over a hospital, and confusing them leads students to misattribute rules. AHRQ generates and distributes the evidence - it funds the studies and builds the toolkits - but it cannot revoke anyone's standing. An accreditor inspects and can withdraw accreditation; a state board holds an individual nurse's license; the FDA controls what products may be sold at all. Knowing which lever each body actually holds tells you what happens when a requirement is ignored.

### Question 4

A restaurant makes the split obvious. Effective means the food does what food is supposed to do - it is nourishing and it is what you ordered. Safe means the kitchen did not give anyone food poisoning or leave glass in the salad. A superb meal can still make you sick, and a bland one can be perfectly safe, so a health inspector and a food critic grade different things. Health care separates its six aims for the same reason: each names a distinct way care can fall short, and fixing one does not automatically fix another.

### Question 5

Two cars end up with identical dents. One driver ran a red light; the other was legally parked when a limb fell in a storm. The damage looks the same, but only one was avoidable by doing something differently, and only that one tells you what to change. Preventability asks whether a known step existed and was skipped or botched - not how bad the outcome looks, and not who ends up embarrassed. Safety teams sort events this way because improvement effort only has traction on the pile where a step was actually available.

### Question 6

Harm from health care used to be like a leak behind a wall: widely suspected, never measured, so nothing forced a response. To Err Is Human measured the puddle, and the estimate was large enough that the debate stopped being about whether the leak was real. Just as important, it changed the question from 'who was careless?' to 'why does this pipe keep bursting in the same place?' That reframing is what turned scattered concern into a research field with funding behind it.

### Question 7

Four kinds of rule-makers operate at once, and each carries a different consequence for breaking it. Statutes come from a legislature, and violating them exposes you to legal penalties. Accreditation standards come from a voluntary body, and violating them threatens the organization's accredited status and the payment that depends on it. Employer policy binds you as an employee, and ethical principles bind you as a professional even when no rule is written down. 'The hospital requires it' and 'state law requires it' therefore describe genuinely different obligations.

### Question 8

A flat tire from a nail in the road is the road's doing; a flat tire because the shop never tightened the valve stem is the shop's doing. Getting sicker from an illness that is running its course belongs to the first category, while a new injury that appeared because a scheduled step was skipped belongs to the second. Patient safety claims only the second category. Repositioning on a schedule is precisely the kind of established safeguard whose omission converts an outcome from unfortunate into preventable.

### Question 9

A leading question invites agreement rather than information; a medicated, drowsy, or hard-of-hearing patient will often nod at whatever name is offered. Asking openly - 'tell me your name and date of birth' - forces the patient to supply the data, which you then match against the label or order already in your hand. Two independently supplied facts checked against a source document is a different act from one nod. And because you cannot reliably judge from the doorway who is alert enough to be trusted, the standard applies to everyone rather than to a selected subset.

### Question 10

Being careful is you watching where you step. Safety is that plus a handrail, adequate lighting, and carpet that is not loose - conditions that hold even on the day your attention lapses. A system that depends entirely on everyone being careful will eventually injure someone, because attention is a finite resource and shifts are long. The formal definition names both halves deliberately: design the environment so the safe action is the easy one, and still expect competent individual performance within it. It counts staff injuries too, since an injured nurse cannot care for anyone.

### Question 11

Judging a bridge only by counting the cars that have already gone off it produces real data that arrives far too late to help. The corrosion, the cracked bolt, and the missing guardrail are all visible long before anything falls, and those are the measurements that let you intervene. This is the difference between lagging indicators, which confirm what already went wrong, and leading indicators, which flag conditions likely to produce harm. Building risk reduction into the definition of safety is what obligates an organization to track the second kind.

### Question 12

Any intervention powerful enough to change physiology is powerful enough to produce effects nobody wanted. If the standard were literally zero risk, the only compliant hospital would be one that treats nobody, which would cause far more harm than it prevented. So the definition splits risk in two: the portion built into a correctly delivered, indicated treatment is disclosed, monitored, and minimized, while the portion created by skipped or mishandled steps is targeted for elimination. 'Acceptable minimum' is not a tolerance for injuring people; it is an honest statement that helping is never entirely risk-free.
